summary: Castine's Dice Head light, ordered by Congress in 1828 at the entrance to Castine Harbor; moved to a shore skeleton tower in 1937 and back to the old tower in 2008.

structures.note: NELH: 42 feet from base to focal plane (12.8 m). The USLHS record gives 51 ft (15.5 m) from base to the centre of the lantern, a different measure, not an error.
Navigational light moved to a skeleton tower closer to the shore (NELH); toppled in September 2007.

NELH: one-and-one-half-story rubblestone dwelling; roof burned April 1999, repaired by September 2000. USLHS record: keeper's quarters dated 1829, wooden colonial cape. The two accounts do not match (see resolved_conflicts).

access.note: Town-owned. Grounds open to the public daily until sunset, with a path around the tower (New England Lighthouses). The sources read do not say whether the tower itself is open to visitors.

events.note: NELH: a newspaper notice of 5 November 1828 said the light would go into service that evening. The clippings file and the USLHS record say 1829.
Act of 18 August 1856 authorised the Treasury to discontinue the light if it decided the light was unnecessary. Not carried out.
NELH: the Lighthouse Board considered discontinuing the light around 1857.
Major repairs (NELH); clippings file header 'rebuilt in 1858'. Six-sided wooden sheath around the tower.
Fourth-order Fresnel lens replaced the lamps and reflectors (NELH).
1,000-pound bell provided and hung, to be rung by hand in answer to signals (Board report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1891, cite 10). NELH dates the bell to 1890 (cite 2).

Keeper Vurney L. King rescued a woman marooned on a rock by the tide, 'on July 23'. The passage gives no year; it appears in the Bulletin issue of 1 September 1931, so 1931 is inferred from that issue.
Navigational light moved to a skeleton tower closer to the shore (NELH).
Old tower turned over to the Town of Castine (NELH).
April 1999 late-night fire through the roof of the keeper's dwelling; repaired by September 2000 (NELH).
A windstorm, which NELH calls a microburst, toppled the skeleton tower in September 2007 (NELH).
A 250 mm optic went into service on 1 January 2008 in the old tower, exhibiting a white flash every 6 seconds (NELH).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1828 Act appropriated the money. NELH dates the first lighting to a 5 November 1828 newspaper notice. The clippings file and the USLHS record say 1829. The story gives both dates and does not choose.

NELH gives 42 feet from base to focal plane (12.8 m). The USLHS record gives 51 feet (15.5 m) from base to the centre of the lantern. These are different measures of one tower, so the story gives both and does not treat either as an error.
NELH describes a rubblestone dwelling; the USLHS record gives a 1829 wooden colonial cape. The story states both.
The USLHS record gives 'granite rubblestone / brick lining'; NELH gives a conical rubblestone tower. The two are compatible, so there is no correction. The story uses NELH's wording.

NELH dates the 1,000-pound bell to 1890. The Board's report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1891 (July 1890 to June 1891) records it as provided and hung. The story gives the report's year range and NELH's date.
The record notes that sources differ on whether the light is still lit. NELH reports the 250 mm optic in service from 1 January 2008, flashing every six seconds, so the light is active.
The first keeper is Sherburne in the USLHS roster and Shelburne in NELH (which also lists 1829-1837, against the roster's 1828). The story uses the roster spelling and gives NELH's.

corrections.why: The record's own quarters fields are filled in (year 1829, style COLONIAL CAPE, construction WOOD), yet its 'Keeper's Quarters?' field says No. NELH describes a one-and-one-half-story rubblestone dwelling still standing. Needs human review: the record and NELH disagree on the dwelling.

notes_for_editor: Sources read: the 1828 Act (primary, scan of the act text); the clippings file (unsigned, undated extracts, cited as such; the 1856 authority and the 1829/1858 header are in it; its 'lenses have been placed in them' passage is undated, so the story does not date it); Lighthouse Board reports 1895, 1896-97, 1899 (scan pages) and the fiscal-1891 report (scan pages 50-51, bell entry; OCR is poor, so the evidence quote is the OCR text as read and the story paraphrases it; printed page numbers not confirmed against the image); the 1 September 1931 Lighthouse Service Bulletin (PDF page 33, commendation for the rescue; the rescue passage gives no year); the USLHS place record (roster matched by name and position, 0.32 km); the NRHP nomination for Castine Historic District (the quoted sentence is legible; the nomination's ID 73000240 is taken from the record and not printed in the OCR). NELH is the main secondary source for the 1828 notice, the 1835 Hunter letter, the 1838 inspection, the 1843 Lewis report, the keeper's autobiography, the 1858 repairs and the 1935-2008 history. The Hunter, Lewis, 1838 and autobiography passages were read only as NELH quotes them; none has been checked against a primary copy. The 1937 move and the 1935 electrification come from NELH only. The 1890 fog-bell date is NELH's; the Board report for the fiscal year to June 1891 records the bell as provided and hung in that year. The station record's 'Keeper's Quarters? No' conflicts with its own quarters fields (see corrections). Beatrice Spurling is named only as NELH's 1974 interviewee; her connection with the station was as a child before 1930. The Castine keeper's house has a private resident (NELH names an artist); she is not named. Chronicling America was searched (28 Maine hits) but no page was read in time; no story claim depends on newspapers beyond the 1828 notice as NELH prints it. The USCG historian's page was blocked (HTTP 403 on the archived copy) and not used. The story says nothing about whether the tower may be climbed (no source read gives it); the NELH access note covers the grounds only.
